'''John C. Mallinson''' (30 January 1932 – 24 December 2015) was a British physicist who made significant contributions to the understanding of [[magnetism]] and [[magnetic recording]].<ref>[https://photos.aip.org/history-programs/niels-bohr-library/photos/mallinson-john-a1 AIP photograph of John C. Mallinson]</ref><ref name=achievement /><ref name=obit/><ref>[https://www.facebook.com/groups/478847068986311 Facebook Group: Dr. John C. Mallinson  - recollections]</ref>  He is perhaps best remembered for his theoretical work on structures with one-sided magnetic flux.<ref name=one_sided>[https://web.archive.org/web/20190826081722/https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/95dc/7c19d9a12d5690aa25e3d51b4620fb934fc4.pdf J.C. Mallinson, "One-sided Fluxes - A Magnetic Curiosity?", IEEE Trans. Magn., Vol. MAG-9, No. 4, Dec. 1973, pp. 678-682]</ref> Their use is exemplified in the [[Halbach array]] and in the familiar [[refrigerator magnet]].

== Personal life ==
Mallinson was born on 30 January 1932 in Bradford, Yorkshire, UK. He attended [[University College, Oxford]] and graduated in 1953 with BA and MA degrees in Natural Philosophy (physics), and an honorary doctorate in 1997. On graduating, he joined the [[Royal Air Force]] for a 3-year term, advancing to pilot a [[English Electric Canberra|Canberra bomber]].<ref name=recollections>[https://www.computerhistory.org/collections/catalog/102792052 Computer History Museum: J. C. Mallinson, "Recollections", 2011]</ref> He remained interested in aviation, and practiced [[aerobatics]] over [[Half Moon Bay, California]]. He volunteered at the [[Hiller Air Museum]] at the [[San Carlos, California]], airport.<ref name=obit>{{Cite web |url=http://ieeemagnetics.org/files/IEEEMS-N-56-2-final.pdf |title=John Mallinson Obituary, Magnetics Society Newsletter, Vol. 56, No. 2, Apr. 2016, page 6 |access-date=2019-08-27 |archive-date=2021-01-17 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210117190949/https://ieeemagnetics.org/files/IEEEMS-N-56-2-final.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>[https://www.computerhistory.org/collections/catalog/102792051 Computer History Museum: John Mallinson Interview]</ref>  Mallinson died in December 2015 following a stroke. He had two daughters, Caroline and Elizabeth and several grandchildren.

== Career ==
In 1956, Mallinson emigrated to the United States to join [[AMP Incorporated]] in [[Harrisburg, Pennsylvania]], where he studied the magnetic properties of [[Ferrite (iron)|ferrites]]. In 1962, he moved to the west coast to join Ampex Corporation in [[Redwood City, California]], rising to become the director of the Recording Technology Department. The department included other major contributors in magnetic recording such as [[Charles Coleman (engineer)|Charles Coleman]] and [[Neal Bertram]].<ref>[http://cmrr.ucsd.edu/research/faculty-profiles/bertram.html UCSD Faculty: Professor Neal Bertram]</ref> Mallinson was called upon as an expert in the long term archival properties of magnetic tape.<ref>[https://archivaria.ca/index.php/archivaria/article/view/11310/12250 J.C. Mallinson, "Preserving Machine-Readable Archival Records for the Millennia"], Archivaria {{ISSN|1923-6409}}, pp.  147-153</ref>  Also at Ampex, Mallinson developed the theory for structures with one-sided magnetic flux.<ref name=one_sided /> One such structure is the [[Halbach Array]] which provides a means of generating powerful, well-confined magnetic fields with [[permanent magnets]]. The familiar decorative [[refrigerator magnet]] also takes advantage of one-sided flux. Also at Ampex, Mallinson oversaw the development of [[PRML]], a new readback technique for magnetic recording.<ref>[https://www.computerhistory.org/collections/catalog/102741157 Computer History Museum: Ampex PRML Prototype]</ref>

In 1984, Mallinson left Ampex to become the founding director of the new Center for Magnetic Recording Research (CMRR)<ref>[https://cmrr.ucsd.edu/ Center for Magnetic Recording Research, UC San Diego]</ref><ref>[https://cmrr.ucsd.edu/_files/newsletters/old-series/vol1-84.pdf CMRR Report Vol. 1, 1984: Inaugural issue]</ref> at [[UC San Diego]]. He was appointed adjunct professor in 1987. By 1990, the Center boasted eight professors and 36 graduate students.

Upon leaving CMRR in 1990, Mallinson taught a course on Magnetism and Magnetic Recording and also took advantage of teaching and research opportunities overseas.  In 1993 and 1995, Mallinson was a visiting professor at [[KTH Royal Institute of Technology]] in Stockholm, Sweden and was appointed permanent visiting professor in 1996. In 1994, he was a visiting professor at the [[University of Twente]] in [[Enschede]], [[The Netherlands]].  Also in 1996, he was a distinguished visiting professor, [[Sony]] Sabbatical Chair in [[Yokohama]], Japan. From 1998 through 2005, he was a regular visiting professor at [[Plymouth University]], UK,<ref name=achievement /> where he collaborated with Hazel Shute and David Wilton. In particular they were able to extend the 2D one-sided flux configurations into 3-dimensions.<ref>[https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/825805/ H. Shute, J. Mallinson, D. Wilton, D. Mapps, "One-sided fluxes in planar, cylindrical, and spherical magnetized structures", IEEE Trans. Magn.. Vol. 36, No. 2, pp. 440 - 451, March 2000 ]</ref>

== Books ==
Mallinson is the author of four textbooks:
* “The Foundations of Magnetic Recording", Academic Press (1987)
* “The Foundations of Magnetic Recording:, Academic Press (2nd edition, 1993), Maruzen Publishing (Japanese edition) (September 1994)
* “Magneto-Resistive Heads, Fundamentals and Applications", Academic Press (1996), Maruzen Publishing (Japanese edition) (September 1996)
* "Magneto-Resistive and Spin Valve Heads: Fundamentals and Applications (Electromagnetism)", Academic Press; 2nd edition (September 2001), Maruzen Publishing (Japanese edition) (June 2002)
* "Recollections", a collection of short autobiographical stories, unpublished, 2011<ref name=recollections/>

Mallinson has published many scientific papers and several contributed book chapters.<ref>[https://www.researchgate.net/scientific-contributions/2035814144_John_C_Mallinson John Mallinson publications]</ref>

== Honours and awards ==
Mallinson became a [[Fellow of the IEEE]] in 1982 for "contributions to the theory of magnetic recording". He was selected as the [[IEEE Magnetics Society]] Distinguished Lecturer for 1983–4 on the topic of "The Next Decade in Magnetic Recording".<ref>[https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/stamp/stamp.jsp?arnumber=1467962 IEEE Magnetics Society Distinguished Lecturers, 1980–1998]</ref><ref>[https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/stamp/stamp.jsp?arnumber=1062836 "Distinguished Lecturers' Program", IEEE Trans. Magn., Vol. MAG19, No. 6, p. 2731, Nov. 1983]</ref> In 1984, he was awarded the [[Alexander M. Poniatoff]] Golden Achievement Award for "leadership in the theory and practice of magnetic recording".<ref>"Mallinson receives Ampex's highest award", Ampex Amplifier (magazine), Summer 1984</ref>  In 1997, he was bestowed with a [[Doctor of Science]] degree from [[Oxford University]].  In 2007, he received the [[IEEE Magnetics Society]] Achievement Award for "contributions to the theory, practice and teaching of magnetic recording"<ref name=achievement>[http://www.ieeemagnetics.org/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=92%3A2007-achievement-award&catid=66&Itemid=97 IEEE Magnetics Society Achievement Award: John C. Mallinson]</ref>
